case_study_insert.main_stem: Cedar Ridge Golf Club (CRG) is a partnership in the leisure and golf sector in the Cotswolds, employing a workforce of 41. Founded in 1998 by Nigel Carrow, it uses a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and a members' committee. CRG plans to invest $920,000 in an eighteen-hole course extension and new clubhouse, financed by a $520,000 bank loan and $400,000 from the sale of an old driving range. It has fixed costs of $390,000 a year, a variable cost of $30 a unit and a selling price of $95, and produces 12,500 units a year in paid rounds of golf. CRG faces labour turnover among greenkeeping staff and complaints about course maintenance from members.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: CRG recorded 3,200 paid rounds, a 6% fall on the previous year, and median tee-time waiting rose from 8 to 19 minutes. Member complaints increased from 14 to 37 per month, with 58% about bunker condition. A survey of 300 members found 44% would pay $6 more for improved course quality. Twelve of 41 staff left in the year; external greenkeeping training at the college costs $1,250 each while on-site coaching is free. Average session length was 4.5 hours.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Cedar Ridge Golf Club as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Leisure Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate rose from 4.25% to 5.0%, raising debt-service costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.00 to $13.72 per hour from April 2026. (3) Energy, water and fertiliser input costs have risen 10.6% year-on-year, while consumer spending on leisure and golf grew 3.8%.

questions.question_text: CRG plans to fund part of its $920,000 course extension with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for CRG of using the $400,000 from the sale of an old driving range instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Cash from selling the old driving range brings $400,000 with no interest charges or capital repayments, protecting CRG's cash flow while it already carries fixed costs of $390,000 a year. The money saved can be spent on tackling the greenkeeping labour turnover and the 58% of complaints about bunkers, protecting the $95 green fee and the 12,500 paid rounds sold.

Point 2: The sale does not pledge the new clubhouse or course as security, so the $920,000 investment cannot be repossessed if rounds fall short. Because CRG is a partnership with a members' committee and democratic leadership, the partners can agree quickly on how to use the proceeds without a bank's conditions. The old range was underused, so converting it into cash releases an asset that was not generating enough rounds; the smaller $520,000 loan that remains is therefore easier to service from contribution of $65 a round.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of sale of assets over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to CRG's $400,000 asset sale, $920,000 expansion and cash flow.

valid_app_words: sale of an old driving range

questions.question_text: CRG wants to attract more players to the extended course. Consider a members' referral incentive, local newspaper and radio advertising, or social media campaigns. Which should CRG choose to promote the extension? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Members' referral incentive: Offering existing members a free round or discount for bringing a newcomer uses CRG's loyal customer base to fill the extra eighteen holes at little cost. It directly targets golfers already in the catchment and suits the 44% of 300 surveyed members who would pay $6 more for quality. However, it grows slowly and mainly rewards current members rather than reaching new golfers beyond the club, so it may not deliver the volume the $920,000 extension needs.

Local newspaper and radio advertising: Print and radio around the Cotswolds can reach local golfers cheaply and publicise the new clubhouse, combining well with the 3,200 rounds currently sold. The messages are short-lived and untargeted, with many readers and listeners never playing golf; with waiting times already up from 8 to 19 minutes, advertising more demand without extra capacity management could frustrate members.

Social media campaigns: Targeted social ads and short course videos can reach golfers across the region and beyond, at low cost per enquiry, and can respond to the 58% of complaints about bunkers by showing the improved course. Results depend on consistent content and may take time to convert, but they scale better than print.

Recommendation: CRG should choose social media campaigns, supported by a modest members' referral incentive. Social media reaches the wider market needed to justify a $920,000 extension at low cost; local print and radio are rejected as untargeted and short-lived, while referrals alone are rejected as too slow and inward-looking to fill the new course.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States simple promotional ideas with little reference to CRG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CRG with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of CRG's membership, complaints and expansion with a justified recommendation that rejects the alternatives.

questions.question_text: CRG has labour turnover among greenkeeping staff and complaints about course maintenance. Explain two benefits for CRG of its democratic leadership style in addressing these issues.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 41 employees and the members' committee discuss how the course is maintained, so greenkeepers can suggest practical fixes for the 58% of complaints about bunkers. Being consulted raises job satisfaction and commitment, which should reduce the twelve staff who left and the disruption that damages course condition; this protects the 3,200 paid rounds and the $95 fee.

Point 2: Consulting members and staff also builds support for the $920,000 extension, because those who help plan the eighteen-hole course are more likely to value it. Better information flow in a hierarchical structure means maintenance problems are reported early, cutting the 37 monthly complaints and helping the partnership achieve the $65 contribution on each of 12,500 rounds instead of spending on external greenkeeping training at $1,250 each.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to CRG's turnover, complaints, rounds and expansion.

questions.question_text: CRG must improve greenkeeping standards. Consider on-site coaching by senior greenkeepers or external college training at $1,250 each. Which should CRG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-site coaching: Senior greenkeepers can teach the exact bunker and turf routines needed at CRG at no cash cost, while keeping all 41 staff on the course during the 3,200-round season. This directly targets the 58% of complaints about bunker condition and the twelve staff who left, with no loss of working time. Its limits are that senior staff lose some of their own output, bad habits can spread, and there is no certificate, which matters if members demand visible standards after complaints rose to 37 a month.

External college training: The $1,250 course gives structured, up-to-date greenkeeping skills and a recognised qualification, which could raise standards across the whole team and support the $920,000 course extension. For twelve workers the cost would be $15,000, affordable beside the expansion. However, it removes staff from the course during busy periods, and generic content may not match CRG's own maintenance routines, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: CRG should choose on-site coaching first, with short college modules for the most senior greenkeepers. Coaching is free, course-specific and avoids losing staff time while labour turnover is a problem. Full college training is rejected because $15,000 and lost greenkeeping hours would hurt course condition just as the extension opens, and the skills can be topped up later.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little reference to CRG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of CRG's costs and course condition.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in the context of CRG with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CRG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $390,000 ÷ ($95 − $30) = $390,000 ÷ $65 = 6,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 6,000 rounds a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $95 − $30 = $65. Answer: contribution per unit is $65.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CRG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 6,000-unit break-even output with 12,500 rounds played to confirm the club is profitable, giving a margin of safety of 6,500 rounds, which supports the $920,000 course extension.
2. Use the $65 contribution to model the $6 price rise that 44% of members would accept: at $101, contribution becomes $71 and break-even falls to $390,000 ÷ $71 = 5,493 rounds, showing the value of quality improvements.
3. Use fixed costs of $390,000 and $65 contribution to set the annual round target needed to service the $520,000 loan on the new clubhouse.
4. Benchmark unit cost ($390,000 ÷ 12,500 + $30 = $61.20 a round) each quarter to detect the maintenance waste behind the 58% bunker complaints and judge whether the $30 variable cost is rising with 10.6% energy, water and fertiliser inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 6,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $65 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 6,500 against 12,500 rounds; modelling the $6 quality premium; loan-service target for the $520,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $61.20 to tackle maintenance waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CRG's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CRG's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.28 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.15 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $20,000 inventories + $55,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $135,000; 2025 current assets = $35,000 + $70,000 + $45,000 = $150,000. 2024 short-term cover = $135,000 ÷ $90,000 = 1.50; 2025 = $150,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.50. The inventory-excluding measure for 2024 = ($135,000 − $20,000) ÷ $90,000 = $115,000 ÷ $90,000 = 1.28; for 2025 = ($150,000 − $35,000) ÷ $100,000 = $115,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.15.

Evaluation: The headline liquidity position is unchanged but its quality has deteriorated. Cover of short-term obligations stays at 1.50 in both years because current assets and current liabilities rose together, from $135,000 to $150,000 and from $90,000 to $100,000. However, cash fell from $60,000 to $45,000 while inventories rose from $20,000 to $35,000 and receivables from $55,000 to $70,000. The inventory-excluding measure fell from 1.28 to 1.15, showing that the unchanged headline depends more on stock. This is concerning while CRG plans a $920,000 expansion and holds a $520,000 loan.

Conclusion: CRG's financial position has not improved. The current ratio is flat at 1.50 and the acid test ratio has fallen from 1.28 to 1.15, revealing weaker underlying liquidity. The fall in cash is the main risk, so the partnership should control stock and receivables before funding more of the extension with debt.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of cash, inventories and liabilities and a justified conclusion on the flat headline ratio.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CRG of introducing an online tee-booking system with contactless payments.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Online booking and contactless payment let members reserve the 3,200 rounds and new eighteen-hole slots at any time, cutting the queue time that rose from 8 to 19 minutes and improving the experience behind 58% of complaints. Faster payment also reduces cash handled by 41 staff and improves cash flow, helping service the $520,000 loan while the $95 green fee is protected.

Disadvantage: Setting up the system costs money and technical skills that a 41-person partnership may lack, and some older members may prefer booking by phone, causing resentment. It also does not by itself fix the bunker condition behind 37 monthly complaints, and if demand exceeds course capacity, online booking could simply fill tee times faster and increase pressure on greenkeeping staff rather than adding value.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to CRG's rounds, waiting times, complaints and staffing.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 10.6% rise in input costs will affect CRG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If CRG's $520,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $520,000 = $3,900 a year (0.0075 × $520,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $390,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the extra cost is zero. Higher rates may reduce discretionary spending on golf, but CRG can limit the risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.72 per hour): With a workforce of 41, greenkeeping and bar roles are often hourly paid, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours or individual pay, so a defensible annual total cannot be invented. The honest comparison is with given productivity: 12,500 rounds ÷ 41 staff = about 305 rounds per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or the extended course raises rounds; otherwise the $65 contribution per round falls.

Input cost inflation (10.6% in energy, water and fertiliser): The $30 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound can be stated: if the whole variable cost rose 10.6%, that adds 10.6% × $30 = $3.18 a round, or about $39,750 a year at 12,500 rounds (12,500 × $3.18). Even a smaller increase would cut the $65 contribution, and it applies to every round played while maintenance complaints are already high.

Conclusion: The 10.6% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 12,500 rounds and directly erodes the $65 contribution needed for the $920,000 extension. The interest rise is about $3,900 and can be fixed, and the wage rise can be offset by productivity of about 305 rounds per worker, whereas course input inflation has no immediate offset.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies external changes with limited application to CRG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on CRG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of CRG with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the other two.
